data.title: Ostrá skala above Vyšný Kubín – a Celtic and Slavic hillfort in Orava
data.excerpt: Ostrá skala north of Vyšný Kubín, right beside the Lusatian hillfort on Tupá skala, is shielded from the south by rock faces 50 to 70 m high. The people of the Púchov culture turned it into a strongly fortified centre of three enclosures, and in the 9th century the Slavs restored its defences and held the site — probably as a regional administrative seat — until the 12th century.
data.metaTitle: Ostrá skala above Vyšný Kubín – Celtic and Slavic hillfort
data.metaDescription: Ostrá skala above Vyšný Kubín, shielded by rock faces 50–70 m high, was a Celtic and later a Slavic hillfort in Orava, held until the 12th century.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: North of Vyšný Kubín, right beside the neighbouring hillfort of Tupá skala; protected from the south by rock faces 50–70 m high

keyFacts.label: Three enclosures
keyFacts.value: Lower (behind the gate), middle (the most finds) and uppermost (a rampart with a timber box construction)

keyFacts.label: Fortification
keyFacts.value: A stone wall over 2 m high with a timber palisade, over 3 m with the masonry included; a Slavic rampart shaped like an asymmetrical horseshoe enclosing 2,500 m²

keyFacts.label: Hall building
keyFacts.value: A long building on the highest ground, its roof supported by central posts, with log walls and a reed roof

keyFacts.label: Notable finds
keyFacts.value: A bronze balance arm, three gold staters (2nd century BC), La Tène fibulae, a bone comb of the middle Roman period

keyFacts.label: Source
keyFacts.value: Compiled by Orgoň, after Pavol Čaplovič

timeline.title: Demise of the hillfort on Tupá skala
timeline.description: The Lusatian occupation and its hillfort on the neighbouring Tupá skala were destroyed.

timeline.title: The Celts occupy Ostrá skala
timeline.description: The people of the Púchov culture (a fusion of the Lusatian population with the Celts) built a strong small fort on Ostrá skala, surrounded by a settlement at its foot.

timeline.title: Gold staters
timeline.description: Three gold staters (imitations of Philip's coins) found at the site in the 19th century, attesting to the growth of the settlement agglomeration in the Middle La Tène period.

timeline.title: First catastrophe date (C14)
timeline.description: Carbon analysis of the grillage construction of the upper rampart — the destruction is recorded on neighbouring Trniny as well.

timeline.title: Second dated destruction phase
timeline.description: Carbonised beams from features in the middle enclosure, covered by a levelling layer.

timeline.title: Departure of the Cotini to Pannonia
timeline.description: A sample from the upper rampart (220 ± 45 AD) roughly corresponds to the period of the Marcomannic Wars and the resettlement of the Cotini together with the Marcomanni and the Quadi — some of the Quadi remained in the territory of present-day Slovakia.

timeline.title: The Slavs rebuild the hillfort
timeline.description: The Slavs discovered the strategic position of Ostrá skala, restored the defences and built new dwellings, making use of the remains of the older La Tène fortification.

timeline.title: Sunken dwelling with an oven
timeline.description: An occupation layer with further settlement features and hearths; finds of spurs, scythes, bucket mounts, knives, axes and razors.

timeline.title: Continuity of occupation
timeline.description: Continuity has been demonstrated between the two main chronological horizons in the use of the site.

timeline.title: Later occupation with log construction
timeline.description: Dwellings of log construction (charred remains of beams); the hillfort survived until the 12th century, probably as an administrative seat even in the beginnings of the Hungarian state.

timeline.title: Orava incorporated into the Hungarian state
timeline.description: Orava became part of the early feudal Hungarian state; Orava Castle did not yet exist at that time.

children.text: One of the important Celtic and later Slavic hillforts in the Orava region was Ostrá skala, which lies north of Vyšný Kubín. It stands in the immediate vicinity of another important hillfort – Tupá skala, known above all for its occupation of the Lusatian culture period. On the southern side the hillfort is protected by rock faces 50 to 70 m high, while the northern side has a gentler gradient, which in prehistory was used for the access route.
The Celts on Ostrá skala

The preceding Lusatian occupation and its important hillfort on Tupá skala were destroyed at some point at the end of the Hallstatt period, and in the Middle La Tène period Ostrá skala was taken over by the Celts (or, more precisely, by the people of the Púchov culture, formed by the fusion of the original Lusatian population with the Celts), who built a strong small fort on it. Their settlement then spread around the foot of Ostrá skala. The steep terrain of the site suited them fully, and the added fortifications made it even more inaccessible. The settlement around Ostrá skala supplied the small fort with water, food and labour, while conversely in times of danger the inhabitants could get behind the walls of the defences and find refuge there from their enemies. On Ostrá skala, too, the defensive works depended on a sufficient number of capable defenders, but they no longer offered protection for the livestock, which had to remain at the foot of the hill or in the mountains.

The settlement just mentioned extends in the locality known as Chmelínce, with a spring of drinking water, in the localities of Za lúky and Železný laz with another spring, in Medziskalie (between Ostrá skala and Tupá skala) and partly also in the locality of Janovie lazy with a further spring of permanent water. Sherds of Hallstatt and Púchov culture pottery were found at the settlements. Metal, bone and other tools are absent. A single quernstone with a central hole points to a La Tène origin.

The approach to Ostrá skala led from the area of Medziskalie from the west, along the northern slope by a track (today a footpath); halfway along its length, at a break on the ground, it originally passed through a fortified gateway. This protected entrance to the settlement is marked by a heap of stone, perhaps also by natural bedrock on the lower (northern) side, which the lower earthen rampart adjoins. On the upper side of the timber gate there ran, parallel and just below the stone wall, a more pronounced path, still discernible today, perhaps a berm with a breastwork to protect the gate. Behind the gate lay the lower enclosure, with ground sloping fairly steeply to the north and with the track (footpath) continuing on.

Access to the middle enclosure was provided from the eastern side by a second gate behind the raised circular end of the rampart masonry and the palisade. By building the rampart and palisade masonry up to a height of 3.5 m, and by levelling from the upper side as well, the ground was evened out along the whole length of the palisade as far as the western lookout. In its role as the middle enclosure this space was used for the most varied purposes, and as a result the greatest number of finds occurred here. They mostly lay beneath the upper Slavic layer, but in some places they reached the uppermost level as well. From this we infer that the enclosure was not always level and that the rearrangement of the layers depended on movements of soil in one period or another.
The fairly steep ground sloping to the north was first divided into three parts. The first of them may have been enclosed against its surroundings by a smaller earthen rampart with a timber palisade.

The second space was separated from the previous one by a stone wall more than 2 m high, the greater part of which survives to this day together with the post holes of the original roofed timber palisade. In front of the wall was a stone-laid path, perhaps for fighting at close quarters. The lower part of the timber log palisade was also faced with stone masonry, probably against fire, so that the continuous stone masonry thus reached a height of more than 3 m and formed veritable castle walls. Today the upper part of the masonry has slipped down as far as its foundation, while the remaining masonry is mostly in its original place, buried for the most part under soil. This state of affairs may have come about as a result of more extensive Slavic alterations, when a considerable part of the soil was swept off the enclosure together with abundant Púchov sherd and metal material, which today covers the stone masonry along its whole length.

children.text: Only the third, highest part was enclosed by a high earthen rampart with a timber box construction. The settlement features were arranged in two rows at different heights running N–S, in the manner of a gallery. The upper row reached the highest point of Ostrá skala and its base was carefully levelled. Besides a clear cutting into the sloping ground, the original levelling was also indicated by numerous sherds lying at a single level, as if on the floor of this building. These are sherds of graphite-free, combed vessels; smooth sherds of Hallstatt character were found only to a negligible extent. Massive posts stood along the centre of the building, from which pits dug into the subsoil remain. It appears to be a long building with its roof supported by central posts and reaching down to the ground, at least on the eastern side. It may therefore be a so-called hall form of building, with hearths on a raised base, log walls and a reed roof.

The second row of buildings lay somewhat lower on the steep ground, whose levelling was likewise indicated by sherds, but the necessary span was achieved by setting in supporting posts, whose post holes have also survived. In all, the summit of Ostrá skala consisted of only the two rows of settlement buildings identified, apart from various shelters for horses, dogs and other stock and equipment, all enclosed by a common high earthen rampart and a timber palisade faced with stones.

Among the interesting finds, particular mention should go to a bronze balance arm for weighing precious metals, from the middle enclosure, most often used in measuring out coin blanks. Mention should also be made of the three gold coins – staters – that were found here in the 19th century. They date to the 2nd century BC, that is to the Middle La Tène period, when, after the Hallstatt occupation of Tupá skala, a settlement agglomeration began to develop around Ostrá skala. Both MT staters are very advanced imitations of Philip's gold coins. To put it in perspective, one gold stater was worth 20 drachmas. La Tène fibulae were also found here. The pottery is represented by jugs and amphorae.

The remains of timber and timber structures also allowed dating within absolute chronology, by C14 carbon analysis. Radiocarbon analysis of the grillage construction of the upper rampart allows a first catastrophe date (Trniny, Ostrá skala) around 70 ± 55 AD. The second sample comes from the area of the middle enclosure, where carbonised beams from the destruction of features covered by a levelling layer were found; they date this phase to around 35 ± 40 AD.

While life at Trniny came to an end after the turn of the era, on Ostrá skala it continued. This can be seen in the further development of the pottery, with a markedly different form of decoration on barrel-shaped pots.

A further sample from the timber layer of the upper rampart gives a date of 220 ± 45 AD, which roughly corresponds to the time when the Cotini left for Pannonia (173–180 AD) in connection with the Marcomannic Wars against the Romans. The Cotini are said to have been resettled together with the Marcomanni and the Quadi, but some of the Quadi, as other sources show, remained in the territory of present-day Slovakia. On Ostrá skala the whole northern slope between the upper and the middle rampart was occupied. In the area of the saddle, post holes were identified following a stone-pitched path, along with various earthworks containing sherds of handmade and combed pottery.

At the edge of the middle enclosure, alongside the stone wall, fine La Tène painted pottery was also found. The later Roman period is signalled on Ostrá skala, too, by iron brooches with a grooved catch plate.

An important find of the Late Roman period is a bone comb from the middle enclosure, made up of two semicircular bone plates decorated around the edge with a ladder pattern and, on the straight lower part, with a double wavy line with a meander. The casing of the toothed part, which was held together by iron rivets, is decorated in a similar and very striking way. Ostrá skala has also yielded a loaf-shaped ring of dark green glass, most likely part of a board game.

In the Hallstatt period Ostrá skala may have been an ancillary farming establishment, but only in the Middle La Tène period did it become a centre and gradually the best-known Púchov settlement in Orava in the La Tène and Roman periods.

children.text: The Slavs on Ostrá skala

Ostrá skala was rediscovered as an advantageous strategic position for building a fortification in the 9th century AD by the Slavs, the ancestors of today's population, who once again restored the defences on the hillfort and built new dwellings. The Slavic fortification system of the late 8th and the 9th century made use of the remains of fortifications from the preceding periods. The earlier arrangement of the interior of the hillfort was likewise continued, when a palisade fence divided the fortified settlement into three enclosures with an area of roughly 1.5–2 ha. The rampart, shaped in plan like an asymmetrical horseshoe, protected the highest settlement area, 2,500 m² in extent. The rampart originated in the La Tène period; the Slavs heaped it up higher and set a timber fence into it.

An occupation layer, a sunken dwelling with an oven and further settlement features with hearths date from the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries. Among the finds, mention should be made of three spurs, scythes, bucket mounts, knives, axes, razors and weapons. From a later period, placed chronologically between the 10th century and the turn of the 12th/13th century, dwellings of log construction were recognised in plan (charred remains of timber beams). In the first chronological horizon the fortified settlement probably performed a central administrative function in the region. On the basis of a long-running reassessment of the find context (iron objects – weapons, horse equipment), continuity of occupation from the second half of the 9th century into the 10th century has now been demonstrated. This was the period between the two most important milestones in the early medieval use of this site. It does not, however, reach the same intensity as in the two dominant periods.

The organs of regional administration were probably also concentrated at the hillfort. Orava was incorporated into the early feudal Hungarian state only at some point in the 11th century. Given that the hillfort at Vyšný Kubín survived until the 12th century, we assume that in some form it continued as an administrative seat even in the beginnings of the Hungarian state, since Orava Castle did not yet exist.
Finally, as a bonus, we present a few unique old photographs showing Ostrá skala.
